chapter: Corrections and views on early Black music
title: Comparing James Reese Europe's band with Will Vodery's 807th and jazz in France
summary: White rates Europe's band for entertainment and Vodery's for military music, and discusses who introduced jazz to the French.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I don't want to keep you more in a minute. I was trying to ask, when I was young, the only Negro band I ever heard of is the James Reese Europe band in the Army. Did yours compare? Was it anything bigger or special more than say the band like you had? Well, I don't try to be modest and say mine wasn't as good as this. I mean, actually in your opinion. That's right. Was your band in a class better or good?

I'll give you my, I'll give you my own personal appraisal of his band. His band had such entertainers in it as Bill Robinson, Noble Sissel, a few other dancers, a few other singers, a few other people whom in my estimation I considered in the entertainment world. But for martial music and the kind of military music, there was only one Negro band over there that topped my band. And that band was Will Vaudry's band.

The 7th Pioneer Infantry band. 807th Pioneer Infantry, Will Vaudry's. Now you see when, and Will Vaudry was such a great musician all the way around, as well as a wonderful conductor. You couldn't, there was no, there was no classification with James Reese Europe. James Reese Europe around New York gathered around himself, some important boys. And the governor favored James Reese Europe to an extent. They got most publicity out there.
Yeah, they got the most publicity out there.

And the Frenchman's loved James Europe's band for the fun they could create. But not so with Mr. Vaudry's band, the 807th. They had 57 pieces. And they were stationed down at Chamault in General J.G. Hobart's quarters down there. And that was the army headquarters for the ADF in France. But, uh, Eurus Band was never called on for that. They were called on to entertain around through war sectors.
Some people talk like Europe introduced jazz to Europe, that is James Europe's band, because they would jazz up numbers. Do you know anything about that?

I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't say that he didn't. I would say that the first acclaim the Frenchman's really give to anyone for the introduction of jazz over there came through and by the efforts of James Reese Europe. Other than, uh, than after James Reese Europe left the scene, after he was killed, I'll say that the furtherance of this was caused by Noble Sissel. And Noble Sissel carried a wonderful band over there. A wonderful band over there. Twelve pieces. I think Noble Sissel carried 18 people all together over there. Two singers and two dancers and himself, he was quite an entertainer. And his band was made up of fine musicians.
